title: Compounding more and more often
objectives: Find $e$ as the limit of compounding interest more and more often
Value an investment with continuous compounding, $Pe^{rt}$
Compare a continuous rate with a rate paid once a year

screens.title: Compounding more and more often
screens.prose: A bank pays interest on your interest. The more often it pays, the more interest earns interest. We will see where that runs out.
You deposit £1.00 at 100% interest a year. Paid once, you end the year with £2.00. Paid as two halves of 50%, you get $1.5 \times 1.5 = 2.25$, so £2.25.
screens.question: Now interest is paid every second, in 31,536,000 tiny parts. Roughly what do you have after a year?

options.why: You expected tiny payments to add up to less. Each one earns interest on all the interest before it, so more payments never lose.
You expected the extra growth to keep piling up. Each payment shrinks as the number of payments grows, and the two effects nearly cancel.
You treated 31 million payments as 31 million chances to grow a lot. Each one is only a 31-millionth of the year's 100%.

hints.text: Splitting once added 25p. Would splitting much more add a lot more?
Look at the 12 row: each payment is a twelfth of 100%.
Twelve payments give $(1 + \tfrac{1}{12})^{12} \approx 2.61$. Payments every second add only a little on top.

feedback.correct: The total creeps up, but it never reaches £3.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about how much each extra split adds.

explain.text: Each extra split makes every payment smaller, so the gain from splitting shrinks. Twelve payments give about £2.61, and payments every second about £2.72. We will watch this happen next.

screens.prose: Slide $n$, the number of payments a year. Each payment adds $\tfrac{1}{n}$ of the balance, so £1.00 grows to $(1 + \tfrac{1}{n})^n$ pounds. The point P tracks it.

derive.caption: $n$ = {{n}}: £1.00 grows to £{{(pow(1 + 1/n, n)).toFixed(2)}}, a factor of {{(pow(1 + 1/n, n)).toFixed(4)}}

screens.question: Slide $n$ from 1 to 52. What does the value after a year do?

options.text: It rises more and more slowly, and stays under the dashed line
It rises by about the same amount at each step
options.why: You read the first few steps only. From 1 to 2 it gains 25p; from 51 to 52 it gains far less than 1p.
You may have read the flattening as a fall. Every extra payment adds a little; the value never drops.
It still changes after 12, just by less. At 12 it is £2.61 and at 52 it is £2.69.

hints.text: Compare the gain from 1 to 2 payments with the gain from 40 to 41.

feedback.correct: The gains shrink as $n$ grows, and the curve hugs the dashed line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the size of each step as $n$ gets large.

explain.text: You saw the steps shrink: £2.00, £2.25, then £2.61 at 12 and £2.69 at 52. The curve flattens under the dashed line at 2.718. More payments always add, but less each time.

screens.prose: The values settle on one number, called $e$. It is $e = 2.71828\ldots$, and it never ends or repeats. Fill in two rows of the climb towards it.
screens.question: Work out $(1 + \tfrac{1}{n})^n$ for 4 and for 12 payments, to four decimal places.

hints.text: Each payment multiplies the balance by $1 + \tfrac{1}{n}$, and there are $n$ of them.
These two bars are the ones to fill.

feedback.correct: 2.4414 and 2.6130: the climb slows as it nears $e$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by $1 + \tfrac{1}{n}$, $n$ times.

byKey.r2c1: Check the 4 row. Each payment is 25%, so the factor is $1.25^4$: four multiplications by 1.25.
byKey.r3c1: Check the 12 row. Keep $1 + \tfrac{1}{12} = 1.083333$ in full; rounding it to 1.0833 first gives 2.6121.

explain.text: You found 2.4414 and 2.6130. The bars climb towards 2.71828..., the number $e$. At 100% a year, compounding without limit turns £1.00 into $\text{£}e$, about £2.72.

screens.prose: Now the rate is 10% a year. With $n$ payments, each adds $\tfrac{0.1}{n}$ of the balance, so £100.00 grows to $100(1 + \tfrac{0.1}{n})^n$.

state.caption: £100.00 at 10% a year, paid in $n$ equal parts

screens.question: As $n$ grows without limit, which value do the bars settle on?

options.why: You used the 100% limit. The rate is now 10%, so the bars stay near £110, nowhere near £271.
You multiplied $e$ by the rate. That is less than the £100.00 you started with.
That is one payment a year, the first bar. The other bars are already above it.

hints.text: Which of the options is close to £110.52, the 365 bar?
The 365 bar shows £110.52, and the bars barely move after it.
Work out $e^{0.1}$: it is 1.10517. So $100e^{0.1} = 110.52$, matching the last bar.

feedback.correct: At 10%, compounding without limit gives a factor of $e^{0.1} = 1.1052$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each option with the 365 bar.

explain.text: At 100% the limit was $e$; at 10% it is $e^{0.1} = 1.1052$. Daily payments already give £110.52, the same to the penny. A rate $r$ compounded without limit multiplies by $e^r$ each year.

screens.prose: Interest paid without limit is called **continuous compounding**. Each year multiplies by $e^r$. £1,000.00 is invested at 5% a year for 10 years.
screens.question: What is it worth after 10 years with continuous compounding?

hints.text: One year multiplies by $e^{0.05}$. What do ten years do?
The daily bar is £1,648.66. Continuous will be a few pence more.
Ten years multiply by $(e^{0.05})^{10} = e^{0.5} = 1.648721$. So the value is £1,648.72.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply by $e^{0.05}$ once for each of the 10 years.

byKey.yearly: That is $1000 \times 1.05^{10}$, paid once a year. Continuous compounding pays a little more.
byKey.one-year: You applied one year only. Ten years multiply by $e^{0.05}$ ten times.
byKey.times-ten: You multiplied by 10 instead of compounding for 10 years. The years multiply the power, not the answer.
byKey.simple: That adds 5% of £1,000.00 each year, with no interest on interest.

explain.text: You multiplied by $e^{0.05}$ ten times: $(e^{0.05})^{10} = e^{0.5}$. That gives £1,648.72, just 6p more than paying daily. Over $t$ years the factor is $e^{rt}$.

screens.prose: Two accounts take £10,000.00 for one year. Account A pays 6% compounded continuously. Account B pays 6.2% once, at the end of the year.

state.caption: £10,000.00 in each account for one year

screens.question: Which account pays more after one year?

options.text: A, because continuous compounding always beats paying once
options.why: You let the compounding decide on its own. $10000e^{0.06} = 10618.37$, so A pays £10,618.37, less than B.
You treated 6% continuous as worth 6.2% a year. $e^{0.06} = 1.0618$, so it is worth 6.18% a year.

hints.text: Work out each account's value after a year.
A multiplies by $e^{0.06}$; B multiplies by 1.062.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute both values before you decide.

byKey.a: You assumed more frequent compounding wins every time. It only adds about 0.18% here, and B's rate is 0.2% higher.

explain.text: Continuous compounding turns 6% into $e^{0.06} = 1.0618$, so 6.18% a year. B's 6.2% beats it by £1.63. Compare the yearly factors, $e^r$ against $1 + r$, before you decide.

screens.prose: Every time, you split a yearly rate $r$ into $n$ payments and let $n$ grow. One year's factor settled on $e^r$, so $t$ years give $e^{rt}$: $$\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} \to e^{rt}, \qquad A = Pe^{rt}$$
screens.question: In $A = Pe^{rt}$, how do you enter a rate of 4% a year?

options.why: You typed the percentage. $e^{4}$ is about 54.6, so each year would multiply the money by 54.6.
You used the yearly growth factor. In $e^{rt}$ the rate goes in alone; the factor comes out as $e^{0.04}$.

hints.text: On the 5% screen, what number sat in the power?

feedback.correct: The rate goes in as a decimal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how 5% appeared in $e^{0.05}$.

explain.text: You used $e^{0.05}$ for 5% and $e^{0.1}$ for 10%. The rate always goes in as a decimal. Then $e^{0.04} = 1.0408$ is the yearly factor.

screens.prose: Why does $(1 + \tfrac{r}{n})^n$ settle on $e^r$? We rename the count so the bracket looks like the one that gave $e$.
screens.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: Let $m = \tfrac{n}{r}$, so $\tfrac{r}{n} = \tfrac{1}{m}$ and $n = mr$: a new name for the count
As $n$ grows so does $m$, and $(1 + \tfrac{1}{m})^m \to e$: the table's limit

hints.text: Start by naming the new count.
Rename, substitute, use the index law, then let $m$ grow.

feedback.correct: The bracket becomes the one from the table, raised to the power $r$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line uses the one above it.

byKey.s3: The index law needs the power $mr$ first, so the substitution comes before it.
byKey.s4: The limit applies once the bracket is $(1 + \tfrac{1}{m})^m$, after the index law.

explain.text: Renaming the count turns $\tfrac{r}{n}$ into $\tfrac{1}{m}$. The index law pulls out $(1 + \tfrac{1}{m})^m$, which tends to $e$. So the whole thing tends to $e^r$.

screens.prose: A money-market desk quotes a deposit rate of 5.00% compounded continuously. A client wants the same deal as a rate paid once a year, which UK banks call the AER (annual equivalent rate).

state.caption: A deposit quote from a money-market desk

screens.question: What yearly rate gives the same growth? Give a percentage to two decimal places.

hints.text: What does one year of continuous compounding at 5% multiply by?
The yearly rate is the factor minus 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the factor $e^{0.05}$, then take away 1.

byKey.same: You kept 5.00%. Continuous compounding earns interest on interest, so the yearly rate is a little higher.
byKey.times-e: You multiplied 0.05 by $e$. The rate goes in the power: $e^{0.05}$.

explain.text: One year at 5% continuous multiplies by $e^{0.05} = 1.05127$. So the yearly equivalent is 5.13%. On £2,000,000.00 that is £102,542.19 of interest, not £100,000.00.

ideas: Splitting a rate into more payments always adds, but less each time, so the total settles.
At 100% a year the factor settles on $e = 2.71828\ldots$; at rate $r$ it settles on $e^r$.
Continuous compounding for $t$ years multiplies by $e^{rt}$, with $r$ as a decimal.

formula.name: Continuous compounding
formula.note: $r$ is the yearly rate as a decimal and $t$ is in years.

summary.trap: Continuous compounding does not always beat a higher rate paid once. Compare $e^r$ with $1 + r$.

quiz.prose: £2,500.00 is invested at 4% a year, compounded continuously, for 3 years.
quiz.question: What is it worth at the end?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The factor is $e^{rt}$ with $r = 0.04$ and $t = 3$.

byKey.yearly: That is $2500 \times 1.04^3$, paid once a year. Continuous compounding pays a little more.
byKey.one-year: You used one year. Three years make the power $0.04 \times 3 = 0.12$.

explain.text: Three years at 4% give the power $rt = 0.12$. $e^{0.12} = 1.127497$, so £2,500.00 becomes £2,818.74.

quiz.prose: A rate of 100% a year is paid in 1,000 equal parts.
quiz.question: Which value is closest to $(1 + \tfrac{1}{1000})^{1000}$?

options.why: You took one part as the whole year. There are 1,000 of them, each multiplying by 1.001.
You expected splitting to change nothing. Interest on interest lifts it above 2.
You saw a large power and expected a large answer. The base is barely above 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall where $(1 + \tfrac{1}{n})^n$ heads as $n$ grows.

explain.text: $(1 + \tfrac{1}{n})^n$ climbs towards $e = 2.71828$. At $n = 1000$ it is 2.71692, already close.

quiz.prose: Some central banks have set negative rates. A deposit of £5,000.00 earns $-0.5\%$ a year, compounded continuously, for 2 years.
quiz.question: What is the deposit worth after 2 years?

byKey.sign: You dropped the minus sign. A negative rate shrinks the deposit.
byKey.simple: You took 0.5% off twice, as simple interest. Continuous compounding takes it off a shrinking balance, so a little less goes.

explain.text: The formula works for a negative rate too: $rt = -0.01$. $e^{-0.01} = 0.99005$, so the deposit falls to £4,950.25. This is the edge case: a negative $r$ makes $e^{rt}$ a decay.

quiz.prose: Bank X pays 8% a year, compounded quarterly (2% four times). Bank Y pays 7.9% a year, compounded continuously.
quiz.question: Which bank's yearly growth factor is larger?

options.why: You let continuous compounding win by default. $e^{0.079} = 1.0822$, below X's $1.02^4 = 1.0824$.
You expected the extra compounding to make up the 0.1% exactly. Work out both factors to four places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute both factors.

explain.text: X multiplies by $1.02^4 = 1.08243$ and Y by $e^{0.079} = 1.08220$. Here the higher rate wins, even with fewer payments. It is not a rule: 7.9% continuous beats 8% paid once, since $1.0822 > 1.08$.
